front: In which year was the U.S. Constitution written?
back: 1787. The Constitution was written in 1787, during the period called the Founding Era. It is the oldest written constitution in the world.

front: In which city did the Founders meet to write the Constitution?
back: Philadelphia. Leaders such as George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, James Madison and Alexander Hamilton came to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1787. Their meeting is called the Constitutional Convention.

front: What is the opening part of the Constitution called?
back: The Preamble. The beginning of the Constitution is the Preamble. It explains why the Founders wrote the Constitution and says the people will govern themselves.

front: When it was written in 1787, the Constitution had a Preamble and how many sections?
back: Seven. The original Constitution had a Preamble and seven sections. The 27 amendments added since then are listed after those seven sections.

front: What share of the states must approve an amendment before it is added to the Constitution?
back: Three-fourths. An amendment is a change to the Constitution. It is added only when three-fourths of the states approve it, which today means 38 of the 50.

front: With 50 states today, how many must approve an amendment for it to be added?
back: 38. Three-fourths of 50 is 37.5, so 38 states are needed. Only 27 amendments have ever been added.

front: What are the first ten amendments to the Constitution called?
back: The Bill of Rights. The Founders added ten amendments listing the rights of people living in the United States. Together they are called the Bill of Rights.

front: How many of the 13 original states had to approve the Constitution before it became the law of the land?
back: Nine. The seventh section of the Constitution said nine of the 13 states had to approve it. All 13 had done so by 1790.

front: Which state became the ninth to approve the Constitution, in 1788?
back: New Hampshire. New Hampshire was the ninth state to approve, which met the number the Constitution required. Rhode Island was the last of the 13, in 1790.

front: What does the judicial branch do with federal laws?
back: It reviews them. Each branch has its own power. Congress makes federal laws, the executive branch enforces them, and the judicial branch reviews them.

front: Which branch of government enforces federal laws?
back: The executive branch. The executive branch, led by the President, enforces the laws that Congress makes. The courts then review them.

front: In a market economy, as the study guide describes it, who controls the economy?
back: Not the government: people are free to start businesses. The United States has a capitalist, or market, economy. The government does not control it, and people are free to start a business and make money.

front: According to the Declaration of Independence, everyone has the right to life, liberty and what else?
back: The pursuit of happiness. Thomas Jefferson wrote that everyone has the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. He wrote it in the Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776.

front: How many years after the Declaration of Independence was the Constitution written?
back: Eleven. The Declaration was adopted in 1776 and the Constitution was written in 1787. In between, the country won its independence and found it needed a new government.

front: What is another name for the legislative branch?
back: Congress. The legislative branch is the U.S. Congress. The Constitution gives it the power to make federal laws.

front: How old must a person be to be elected to the House of Representatives?
back: At least 25. A member of the House must be at least 25 and live in the state where the district is. The Senate asks for 30.

front: How old must a person be to be elected to the U.S. Senate?
back: At least 30. A senator must be at least 30 and live in the state they represent. That is five years older than the minimum for the House.

front: According to the study guide, how many voting members does California have in the House of Representatives?
back: 52. California has the most people of any state, so it has the most voting members in the House. States that have more people have more representatives.

front: Which state has only one voting member in the House because it has the fewest people?
back: Wyoming. Seats in the House follow population. Wyoming, the state with the fewest people, has a single voting member.

front: What is a bill?
back: A proposal for a new law. When members of Congress want a new law, they write a bill. It becomes law only after both parts of Congress pass it and the President signs it.

front: If all 435 voting members are present, how many votes does a bill need to pass the House?
back: 218. A bill needs a majority, which means more than half. Half of 435 is 217.5, so 218 votes are needed.

front: How many senators must vote for most bills to pass the Senate, when all 100 vote?
back: 51. A majority of the 100 senators is 51. The same idea applies in the House, where the majority is 218.

front: What is the leader of the House of Representatives called?
back: The Speaker of the House. The leader of the House is called the Speaker. The Speaker is also next in line for the presidency after the Vice President.

front: What do the 435 voting members of the House each come from?
back: A congressional district. Each state is divided into congressional districts. Each district elects one person to serve in the House.

front: Why does the first section of the Constitution describe Congress?
back: The Founders thought making laws the most important power. The Founders believed the power to make laws was the most important power in government. So they described Congress first.

front: What title do most leaders of the executive departments hold?
back: Secretary. Most executive departments are led by a Secretary, such as the Secretary of Homeland Security. The Department of Justice is the exception.

front: What is the leader of the Department of Justice called?
back: The Attorney General. The head of the Department of Justice is not called a Secretary. The title is Attorney General, and it is a Cabinet-level position.

front: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) is part of which executive department?
back: The Department of Homeland Security. Each executive department has many smaller agencies. USCIS is one of them, and it belongs to the Department of Homeland Security.

front: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is part of which department?
back: The Department of Justice. The FBI is one of the agencies inside the Department of Justice. That department is led by the Attorney General.

front: What does it mean that the President is Commander in Chief?
back: The President is in charge of everyone serving in the military. Commander in Chief is the President's role over the Armed Forces. Everyone serving in the U.S. military is under the President's charge.

front: How many branches do the U.S. Armed Forces have, according to the study guide?
back: Six. The guide says there are six branches of the Armed Forces. The President is in charge of all of them as Commander in Chief.

front: In which month do citizens vote for President?
back: November. Presidential elections are held in November. The President is then elected for four years.

front: What are the two major political parties in the United States today?
back: The Democratic Party and the Republican Party. A person running for President is nominated by a political party. The two major parties today are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party.

front: Besides advising the President, what position does the Vice President hold in Congress?
back: President of the Senate. The Vice President works in the executive branch but is also the President of the Senate. The Vice President is a member of the Cabinet too.

front: Who must approve a person the President nominates to be a federal judge?
back: The U.S. Senate. The President nominates federal judges, and the Senate must approve them. Because more than one branch takes part, this is an example of the separation of powers.

front: What are the federal courts below the Supreme Court sometimes called?
back: Lower federal courts. The judicial branch is the Supreme Court and the other federal courts. Those other courts are sometimes called lower federal courts.

front: How many U.S. District Courts are shown in the study guide's chart of the federal court system?
back: 94. The guide's chart shows one Supreme Court, 13 circuits of the Court of Appeals and 94 district courts. The Supreme Court is the highest of them.

front: How many circuits does the U.S. Court of Appeals have in the study guide's chart?
back: 13. Between the 94 district courts and the one Supreme Court sits the Court of Appeals, in 13 circuits. Nine is the number of Supreme Court justices, not of circuits.

front: When can a federal court review a law?
back: Only when a legal case about it is before the court. Courts do not review laws on their own. Someone has to bring a legal case that the court has the authority to hear.

front: What is another word for a judge on the Supreme Court?
back: Justice. Supreme Court judges are called justices. One of them is the Chief Justice of the United States.

front: Can any other court change a decision of the Supreme Court?
back: No. The Supreme Court is the highest court, so its decisions are final. No other court in the United States can change them.

front: What is a treaty?
back: An agreement between two or more countries. Making treaties is a power of the federal government. Treaties can end wars or set up cooperation on matters such as trade.

front: Who has the power to print the money used in the United States?
back: Only the U.S. government. Printing money is one of the powers the Constitution gives to the federal government. States cannot print their own dollars.

front: What is the person in charge of a state's executive branch called?
back: A governor. Each state has its own three branches. The head of a state's executive branch is its governor.

front: Which section of the Constitution explains how new states can join the United States?
back: The fourth section. The fourth section covers the states: how their governments are set up and how new states join. The first three sections set up the federal branches.

front: How does a person come to run for President, according to the study guide?
back: They are nominated by a political party. People who run for President are nominated by a political party. The two major parties today are the Democratic and Republican parties.

front: What happens to a bill right after both parts of Congress pass it?
back: It is sent to the President. A bill passed by the House and the Senate goes to the President. The President either signs it into law or vetoes it.

front: In the study guide, what does the word “veto” mean?
back: The President did not sign the bill. A veto is the President's refusal to sign a bill. The bill then fails unless Congress votes to override the veto.

front: What do the justices write when a majority of them vote the same way on a case?
back: A decision that explains their reasons. After hearing a case the justices meet, discuss it and vote. The majority then writes a decision explaining its reasons.

front: Which of these does the study guide give as an example of the federal government's power to protect the people?
back: Creating an army to defend the nation. The Constitution lets the federal government create an army and declare war if the country is attacked or threatened. Schools and fire departments are state powers.

front: How many rights or freedoms are listed in the First Amendment?
back: Five. The First Amendment lists five freedoms: speech, religion, assembly, the press, and petitioning the government. They belong to everyone living in the United States.

front: Which amendment says a person accused of breaking the law has the right to a trial with a jury?
back: The Sixth Amendment. The Bill of Rights lists more than the First Amendment freedoms. The Sixth Amendment protects people accused of a crime, including the right to a jury that decides guilt or innocence.

front: What is the last day each year to send in federal income tax forms?
back: April 15. Everyone living in the United States must pay income taxes. A federal income tax form is due each year by April 15.

front: Which amendment, added in 1971, says citizens 18 and older can vote?
back: The 26th Amendment. Four amendments are about who can vote. The most recent, the 26th in 1971, set the voting age at 18.

front: Which amendment, added in 1964, says you do not have to pay a poll tax to vote?
back: The 24th Amendment. A poll tax was a charge for voting. The 24th Amendment ended it in 1964.

front: At what moment does an applicant for naturalization become a U.S. citizen?
back: When they take the Oath of Allegiance at the ceremony. Passing the test and interview is not the last step. Applicants become citizens when they raise their right hand and say the Oath of Allegiance at the naturalization ceremony.

front: How old must a person be to become a naturalized U.S. citizen?
back: 18. Being 18 is the first requirement the study guide lists. The others include being a lawful permanent resident and passing the naturalization test and interview.

front: According to the study guide, between which ages must men register for the Selective Service?
back: 18 and 26. Men who are citizens or legal residents must register for the Selective Service. The duty applies between the ages of 18 and 26.

front: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America, created in 1607?
back: Jamestown. England created Jamestown in 1607, which began the Colonial Period. More settlements followed and became the colony of Virginia.

front: Which European country was the first to send ships across the Atlantic Ocean?
back: Spain. In the 1400s some European countries built ships that could cross the ocean, and Spain went first. England, France and Portugal created colonies later.

front: In what year did the Pilgrims create the colony of Massachusetts?
back: 1620. The Pilgrims were English colonists who came in 1620. Many of them came to North America for religious freedom.

front: In what year was the first group of enslaved Africans brought to Jamestown?
back: 1619. Colonists wanted more workers for their farms, and enslaved people were brought from Africa by force. The first group arrived at Jamestown in 1619.

front: Which crops did the Jamestown colonists grow and sell to England?
back: Tobacco and later cotton. After hard first years, the colonists moved to new areas and grew tobacco, and later cotton. They made a lot of money selling these crops to England.

front: In 1707 England and Scotland became one country. What was it called?
back: Great Britain. England and Scotland are both on the island of Britain. After they joined in 1707, the 13 colonies were part of Great Britain.

front: In which years did the American Revolutionary War start and end?
back: 1775 and 1783. The war began in 1775. It ended in 1783, when Great Britain signed a treaty agreeing that the United States was an independent country.

front: Who was named general of the colonial army during the American Revolutionary War?
back: George Washington. When the colonists created an army, George Washington was named its general. This is one reason he is called the Father of Our Country.

front: Where did the British Army surrender in 1781?
back: At Yorktown, Virginia. The fighting stopped in 1781 when the British surrendered at the Battle of Yorktown. The war did not officially end until the treaty of 1783.

front: What did the colonists mean by “taxation without representation”?
back: Britain raised their taxes without letting their representatives vote on it. In the 1760s Britain raised taxes on the colonies to help pay for a war. The colonists thought it unfair that their representatives had no vote on those taxes.

front: What was a colonial congress?
back: A legislative branch that made laws for a colony. Each of the 13 colonies had its own colonial congress to make its laws. Britain later made these congresses illegal, which angered the colonists.

front: In which colony did colonists begin fighting the British in 1775?
back: Massachusetts. The fighting started in Massachusetts in 1775. Soon all 13 colonies were fighting Great Britain.

front: Who negotiated the treaty with Great Britain in 1783 as a diplomat?
back: Benjamin Franklin. A diplomat travels to other countries to represent the United States. Benjamin Franklin negotiated the treaty in which Britain accepted American independence.

front: With what name did the writers of the Federalist Papers sign their essays?
back: Publius. James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay wrote the essays. All three signed them with the single name Publius.

front: How many essays made up the Federalist Papers?
back: 85. The Federalist Papers were 85 essays about the Constitution. They were printed in newspapers between October 1787 and May 1788.

front: Why did many people dislike the Constitution in 1787?
back: It did not include a list of rights. Many people would not support a Constitution with no list of rights. Its supporters agreed to add one, and the Bill of Rights followed in 1791.

front: In which years did George Washington serve as President?
back: 1789 to 1797. When the new government was created under the Constitution, George Washington was elected the first President. He served from 1789 to 1797.

front: For about how long had Native Americans lived in the Americas before Europeans arrived?
back: Around 20,000 years. Native Americans had lived in North and South America for around 20,000 years. There were many tribes, each with its own culture, language and government.

front: What did the 13 original colonies become when the Declaration of Independence was adopted?
back: The 13 original states. By adopting the Declaration of Independence the colonists created the United States of America. Each colony became a state.

front: Why did France sell the Louisiana Territory to the United States in 1803?
back: France needed money to pay for wars in Europe. France was fighting wars in Europe and needed money. The sale gave the United States the land between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains.

front: What was the “Trail of Tears”?
back: The forced move of five Native American nations, on which thousands died. Between the 1830s and 1850s the Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw were forced from their homeland. Thousands died of disease and starvation on the journey.

front: When Texas joined the United States in 1845, which state in order did it become?
back: The 28th. Texas had been part of Mexico until 1836, and then its own country until 1845. It joined the United States as the 28th state.

front: With which country did the United States go to war in 1846 over Texas and land in the southwest?
back: Mexico. This was the Mexican-American War, which the United States won in 1848. Mexico then agreed that Texas was part of the United States and sold its southwestern land.

front: Which was the first state bordering the Pacific Ocean to join the United States?
back: California. California joined in 1850 as the 31st state. With it the country reached from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

front: What did the eleven Southern states that left the United States in 1861 call their country?
back: The Confederate States of America. The Civil War began after eleven Southern states left and tried to form their own country. The Northern states were still called the United States of America.

front: What is Frederick Douglass known for?
back: Escaping slavery and becoming a civil rights leader who spoke and wrote against it. Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery. He became famous for speeches and books about ending slavery and protecting civil rights for all people.

front: What happened to Abraham Lincoln a few days after the South surrendered?
back: He was assassinated. The South surrendered in April 1865, ending the Civil War. A few days later Lincoln was assassinated, which means murdered for political reasons.

front: Which amendment, added on December 6, 1865, says slavery is illegal in the United States?
back: The 13th Amendment. After the Civil War the Constitution was changed to end slavery for good. The 13th Amendment did that in December 1865.

front: What happened on June 19, 1865, the day remembered as Juneteenth?
back: Enslaved people in Galveston, Texas, learned they were free. The people enslaved in Galveston, Texas, were the last to learn that the war was over and they were free. Juneteenth is now a national holiday marking the end of slavery.

front: When did the South surrender, ending the Civil War?
back: April 1865. The Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865. The North won when the South surrendered in April 1865.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What was World War I called when it started?
back: The Great War. The war that began in Europe in 1914 was first called the Great War. It is called World War I today.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: In what year did the United States join World War I?
back: 1917. The war ran from 1914 to 1918, but the United States did not join until 1917. It fought until the war ended on November 11, 1918.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Who was President of the United States during World War I?
back: Woodrow Wilson. Woodrow Wilson was the 28th President, in office from 1913 to 1921. He led the country through World War I.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: How many times was Franklin Roosevelt elected President?
back: Four. Roosevelt was the longest-serving President, in office from 1933 until he died in 1945. The 22nd Amendment later limited a person to being elected twice.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What event started World War II in 1939?
back: Germany attacked Poland. World War II began in Europe in 1939 when Germany attacked Poland. The United States entered two years later, after Pearl Harbor.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Where is Pearl Harbor, the naval base Japan attacked on December 7, 1941?
back: Hawaii. Pearl Harbor is a U.S. naval base in Hawaii. The attack led the United States to enter World War II.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What was the Soviet Union?
back: Russia and the nearby countries it controlled. Russia controlled many nearby countries, and together they were called the Soviet Union. It was the rival of the United States in the Cold War.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: How was the Cold War mostly carried on?
back: With diplomats, spies, information and threats rather than battles between the two sides. American and Soviet soldiers did not fight each other in battles. Each side used diplomats and spies, and built large armies in case war came.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Which country was the first to send a satellite into space, in 1957?
back: The Soviet Union. During the Cold War both sides tried to send rockets into space. The Soviet Union launched the first satellite in 1957, and the United States landed the first person on the moon in 1969.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: When and how did the Cold War end?
back: In 1991, when the Soviet Union collapsed. The Cold War lasted from after World War II until 1991. It ended when the Soviet Union collapsed.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What does the Civil Rights Act of 1964 make illegal?
back: Discrimination based on race, religion, sex or national origin. The civil rights movement convinced Congress to pass two major laws. The first, in 1964, made it illegal to discriminate on these grounds.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What does the Voting Rights Act of 1965 say?
back: States cannot deny people the right to vote based on their race. Some state laws had made it hard for people to vote because of their race. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 says states cannot do that.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta were civil rights leaders from which community?
back: The Latino American community. Many communities helped lead the fight for civil rights. Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta were leaders from the Latino American community.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Where did the fourth hijacked plane crash on September 11, 2001, after its passengers fought the terrorists?
back: Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Two planes hit the World Trade Center and one hit the Pentagon. The passengers on the fourth plane fought back, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: What happened to banks, businesses and jobs during the Great Depression?
back: Banks and businesses closed, and many people could not find work. The Great Depression was the worst time for the economy in American history. Many people lost their jobs, their homes and their money.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: In what year did the United States become the first country to land a person on the moon?
back: 1969. The space race was part of the Cold War. The Soviet Union launched the first satellite in 1957, and the United States reached the moon in 1969.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: In which years did Dwight Eisenhower serve as President?
back: 1953 to 1961. Eisenhower had been a general in World War II. He became the 34th President in 1953, during the Cold War, and served until 1961.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: About how many American Indian tribes are there in the United States today, according to the study guide?
back: Over 500. Native Americans are also called American Indians. The guide says there are over 500 tribes today, and lists some of them, such as the Cherokee and the Navajo.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Between which two Alabama cities did Martin Luther King, Jr., and other leaders organize a march for voting rights in 1965?
back: Selma and Montgomery. The march from Selma to Montgomery supported voting rights for all citizens. Soon after it, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
front: Which award did Martin Luther King, Jr., receive in 1964?
back: The Nobel Prize for Peace. King led peaceful protests against racial discrimination. He was awarded the Nobel Prize for Peace in 1964.

front: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States, in 1886?
back: France. France gave the statue as a symbol of friendship. It has become a symbol of freedom and democracy.

front: What date is on the tablet the Statue of Liberty holds in her left hand?
back: July 4, 1776. The statue holds a torch in her right hand and a tablet in her left. The tablet carries the date the Declaration of Independence was adopted.

front: On the American flag, what is red a symbol for?
back: Bravery. Each color of the flag has a meaning. Red stands for bravery, white for purity and blue for justice.

front: On the American flag, what is blue a symbol for?
back: Justice. Red stands for bravery and white for purity. Blue is the symbol for justice.

front: Who wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner”?
back: Francis Scott Key. Francis Scott Key wrote it about seeing the American flag after a battle during the War of 1812. It is the national anthem.

front: What was Ellis Island?
back: An immigration station in New York Harbor. Ellis Island began receiving immigrants in 1892. Over the next 62 years more than 12 million people arrived through it.

front: Angel Island was an immigration station for people who had crossed which ocean?
back: The Pacific Ocean. Angel Island was on the West Coast. Between 1910 and 1940 it processed nearly a million immigrants who had crossed the Pacific.

front: What do the letters “D.C.” in Washington, D.C., stand for?
back: District of Columbia. The capital is named after George Washington. It is a district controlled by the federal government, between Maryland and Virginia, and is not part of any state.

front: On which day is Martin Luther King, Jr. Day celebrated?
back: The third Monday in January. The holiday honors the life and work of the civil rights leader. It falls on the third Monday in January each year.

front: Why is Presidents' Day celebrated on the third Monday in February?
back: It falls between the birthdays of Washington and Lincoln. George Washington was born on February 22 and Abraham Lincoln on February 12. The holiday honors both, on a Monday between the two dates.

front: What was Memorial Day originally called?
back: Decoration Day. The name came from decorating graves with flowers, wreaths and flags. The day became widely observed soon after the Civil War.

front: What was Veterans Day originally called?
back: Armistice Day. It first marked the end of World War I on November 11, 1918. In 1954 Congress renamed it Veterans Day to honor everyone who has served.

front: What does Thanksgiving celebrate?
back: A harvest meal shared by Native Americans and English colonists in 1621. Thanksgiving is on the fourth Thursday in November. It recalls a harvest feast in 1621 in what became Massachusetts.

front: Which Native American tribe gathered with the English colonists for the harvest feast of 1621?
back: The Wampanoag. The colonists were trying to create a colony in Massachusetts. The Wampanoag gathered with them in the fall for a harvest feast.
